articles.title: Apple's Market Value Grew From $350 Billion to $4 Trillion During Tim Cook's 15 Years as CEO. Here's What That Growth Curve Means for Apple's Next Chapter Under John Ternus
articles.summary: Key PointsApple is highly unlikely to match the returns it produced under Tim Cook over the next 15 years.
articles.excerpt:
At the end of August, Tim Cook stepped down as CEO of Apple (AAPL -0.98%), ending a highly successful tenure as the head of one of the world's largest companies. Tim Cook led Apple as it revolutionized the tech sector and became the world's first trillion-dollar company. Apple is now worth $5.2 trillion, up from just $350 billion when Tim Cook took over -- though it was worth about $4.6 trillion when Cook ended his tenure as CEO. What does that mean for Apple's new leader, John Ternus?

Tim Cook became the CEO of Apple in 2011, four years after the first iPhone was released. Apple's famous smartphone was already a hit, but Tim Cook oversaw the company's creation and launch of several other highly popular products, such as the Apple Watch and the AirPods.

Perhaps more importantly, Tim Cook transformed Apple's installed base into a massive cash-generating machine through millions of paid subscriptions across more than a dozen services. Apple's services segment is now its second-largest by sales, and it carries much juicier margins than hardware products.

articles.author: Apple Newsroom
articles.excerpt:
Apple today announced the launch of the Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States, a virtual research study and associated app designed to advance the understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools. By examining what drives user trust, the quality of responses, comprehension, and everyday health actions, the study aims to inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for Apple and the industry.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness. “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”

The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature.

Bloomberg reports that Apple lifer Corey Fugman will replace Jennifer Bailey as the head of the Apple Pay and Wallet division. Here are the details.

A few months ago, Bloomberg reported that Jennifer Bailey, Apple’s head of Apple Pay and Wallet, who had led Apple Pay since its launch in 2014, would retire in October.

At the time, Apple’s services boss Eddy Cue said internally that the company would announce its succession plan before her transition at the end of October, and that she would “continue to be available to support the transition in an advisory role.”

October came and went without any public announcement on that front. Today, however, Bloomberg reported that Apple has tapped Corey Fugman, “a 26-year company veteran as the new head of its payment service and digital wallet unit.”

According to his LinkedIn profile, Fugman joined Apple in September 2000 as Merchandising Manager for Apple Retail and has held several leadership positions since then, including overseeing Apple Card and Apple Cash from 2019 to 2021.

Most recently, he served as Senior Director of Apple Pay and Wallet, a position he has held since November 2021.

articles.title: Apple reveals new Mac security controls as AI agents raise privacy risks
articles.summary: Following an October announcement, Apple has detailed new permission controls, warnings, and transparency features coming to macOS 27.3 to address risks posed by AI agents and other apps.
articles.author: Sarah Perez
articles.excerpt:
As promised last month, Apple on Monday announced changes to Mac security controls designed to protect users’ data from the growing popularity of AI agents and their apps’ demand for “full disk access.”

“Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk,” Apple warned in its blog post aimed at app developers.

Unlike AI chatbots that simply answer questions, agents run on a user’s device where they can take actions across the operating system, files, and apps on the user’s behalf.

While the tools can be useful, Apple has grown concerned about the increased risks to users’ data and privacy that these AI agents introduce. At the same time, the company has been benefiting from sales of Mac minis and Mac Studio computers that AI early adopters have been purchasing specifically to run their local AI models.

To balance these competing interests, Apple said in October that it would revise some of its security settings around Mac apps. The announcement followed two notable incidents involving AI agents.

articles.title: Epic formally asks SCOTUS to uphold contempt ruling against Apple
articles.summary: Epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Here are the details. more…
articles.author: Marcus Mendes
articles.excerpt:
Epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Here are the details.

As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.

The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.

Although the court largely sided with Apple, it did rule that the company could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple ultimately allowed those links, but imposed new restrictions, including a 27% commission on external purchases, in addition to new rules limiting how developers could display buttons and links to alternative payment methods.

Epic challenged those restrictions, and the court agreed that Apple had violated the original injunction, holding the company in civil contempt.

Apple has since attempted multiple times to overturn that ruling, arguing that the original injunction contained no explicit prohibition on imposing those restrictions.

With the iOS 27.3 beta 2 that was released on Monday, Apple unveiled a cool new feature for iPhone Duo users. I don’t own a Duo, but it’s such a cool feature I’m really hoping Apple brings it to the MacBook.

BEIJING — How does the U.S. stay ahead of China in the artificial intelligence race? Keep advanced chips out of Beijing's reach, or sell weaker versions to keep Chinese companies reliant on American technology?

The consequences for U.S. businesses came into sharper focus after Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO, ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week.

articles.title: Today in Apple history: Apple demands big damages from Samsung
articles.summary: On September 13, 2013, Apple and Samsung headed back to court to determine the amount of damages Samsung would pay for copying the iPhone. (via Cult of Mac - Your source for the latest Apple news, rumors, analysis, reviews, how-tos and deals. )
articles.author: Luke Dormehl
articles.excerpt:
November 13, 2013: Apple and Samsung head back to court to determine how much the Korean company must pay for having copied the iPhone. Apple asks Samsung for $379 million in damages for ripping off key technical and design features.

Cupertino’s lawyers arrive at that number based on estimated lost profits, royalty rates and the $3.5 billion worth of copyright-infringing devices Samsung sold during the period in question.

Apple wasn’t just fighting Samsung over smartphone patents. It was fighting over who deserved credit — and billions of dollars — for inventing the modern smartphone. After watching Samsung churn out Galaxy devices that looked and behaved suspiciously like iPhones, Apple launched an all-out legal assault.

The case became a defining moment in the smartphone wars, exposing just how much of the iPhone’s success came from its design, interface and carefully engineered user experience. It also raised a question that still hangs over the tech industry: Where does inspiration end and copying begin?

Apple’s war with Samsung officially kicked off three years earlier in August 2010. At that time, Apple executives visited Samsung’s HQ in Seoul, South Korea, and gave a presentation with the title, “Samsung’s Use of Apple Patents in Smartphones.”

Foxconn is by far the largest contract manufacturer for iPhones, and at one point the majority of its revenue came from Apple. That hasn’t been true for some time, however, largely because of the company’s rapid expansion into servers for AI data centers and cloud storage.

All the same, some 29% of its revenue still comes from its consumer electronics division, of which Apple is by far the largest customer. It’s likely that at least some of its growth comes from the assembly of Apple products.

articles.title: OLED iPad Air launch is only a few months away
articles.summary: Apple's first OLED iPad Air remains on track for the first half of 2027. Other improvements to the mid-range tablet are also quite possible. (via Cult of Mac - Your source for the latest Apple news, rumors, analysis, reviews, how-tos and deals. )
articles.author: Ed Hardy
articles.excerpt:
Excited about the new OLED iPad mini, but want something larger? Apple’s first iPad Air with an OLED display remains on schedule to arrive in the first half of 2027, according to a new supply-chain report.

The upgrade is expected to bring richer colors and deeper blacks to Apple’s midrange tablet though it supposedly won’t be ale to match the high-end OLED display technology found in the iPad Pro.

In an OLED display, each pixel produces its own light and can switch off completely when displaying black. In contrast, LCD screens rely on separate backlights to illuminate the entire display, making it much more difficult to reproduce true blacks. Another result is stronger colors and better contrast.

Apple is gradually bringing OLED to more products across its lineup, replacing LCD panels as the technology becomes more affordable to manufacture. The iPhone made the transition long ago, while the iPad Pro and Apple Watch also use OLED screens. The OLED trend reached the iPad mini just this month.

A long series of leaks points to the iPad Air as next on the list.

articles.title: Today in Apple history: Microsoft reveals its plans for Windows 1.0
articles.summary: On November 10, 1983, Microsoft told the world about a new product it planned to launch called Windows 1.0. Apple faced a brand-new rival! (via Cult of Mac - Your source for the latest Apple news, rumors, analysis, reviews, how-tos and deals. )
articles.author: Luke Dormehl
articles.excerpt:
November 10, 1983: Microsoft tells the world about an upcoming product called Windows that will bring the graphical user interface to IBM PCs. Although Microsoft’s announcement about the new operating system comes shortly before Apple launches the first Macintosh in January 1984, Windows 1.0 won’t actually ship until November 1985, earning it an early reputation as “vaporware.”

At the time, Apple doesn’t view Windows as much of a threat. That doesn’t take long to change, however.

Microsoft’s first version of Windows looked like a clumsy imitation of the Macintosh‘s operating system. But dismissing it as a bad knockoff would miss the bigger story: Windows didn’t have to be better than Apple’s graphical interface to change the computer industry. It just needed to make the mouse-driven, point-and-click future accessible to the millions of people with IBM-compatible PCs.

Apple’s early confidence that Windows 1.0 posed little threat would prove disastrously misplaced. A seemingly unimpressive $99 product planted the seeds of a rivalry that would shape the next decade of personal computing — and nearly destroy Apple along the way.

When Microsoft first revealed its plans for Windows, Apple had just introduced the GUI to the general public with its ill-fated Lisa computer.
